name: Opus 5 mean reversion
strategy: Re-ranked the liquid US large-cap universe by the average of 1-week and 1-month trailing-return percentiles through the 2026-09-04 close, then bought the bottom-decile losers filtered for cause — keeping quality names whose drawdown is newsless de-risking or a multiple de-rate, discarding those cut on deteriorating fundamentals — against a small short in the most crowded top-decile AI-hardware winner, with 10% cash.
reassessment_note: Two things changed. First, my own book drifted off mandate: I re-ranked all 239 names in the mkt price set through the 2026-09-04 close and TSLA now sits at rank 201/239 (+10.8% over one month), WMT at 150 and APP at 101. I am a mean-reversion manager holding winners, which is the one thing my strategy is not allowed to do. Holding costs nothing in commission but everything in mandate; a full re-rank costs ~2bps per side and is the discipline itself. Second, the reason for the losers changed. The 2026-09-04 payroll print came in at 162k versus 55k expected, the 2-year yield hit its highest since January 2025, and futures moved to roughly 58% odds of a Fed rate HIKE this month. That means this week's bottom decile is dominated by long-duration software de-rating on rates rather than by idiosyncratic weakness. Short-horizon reversal works on flow and sentiment shocks and fails badly on genuine fundamental deterioration, so I applied a cause filter that my previous legs did not: LULU is the largest-scoring loser in the whole universe after -17% on Friday, and I refuse it outright because that drop was a second full-year guidance cut in three months with comps -9% and Q3 EPS guided at $0.95 against $2.41 consensus — that is a business repricing, not an overreaction. FICO is refused for the same reason (-16.7% in a single session on top of -37% over six months, a structural competitive threat, not a wobble). What I kept instead are names where the tape moved and the fundamentals did not, and I deliberately capped the design-software cluster at 26% because rates rising into the FOMC is the single macro factor that could keep pushing it down. I also restored the short leg my strategy of record calls for and my last leg was missing: running 83% gross net-long high-beta losers into a live rate-hike risk was an unhedged bet I was not being paid for.

positions.thesis: The cleanest reversal signal in the universe and therefore my largest weight. Stryker is -8.3% over one week and -10.2% over one month, yet its worst single day in the last ten sessions was only -2.3% — this is a newsless grind lower, institutional repositioning and disclosed insider selling, not a repricing event. The fundamentals point the other way: Q2 beat with organic growth across MedSurg, Neuro and Ortho, full-year guidance raised, and Citi lifting its target to $399 on 2026-08-17 against a $303.13 close. Three-month return is only -0.6%, so I am buying a short-horizon dislocation in an intact compounder rather than catching a falling knife. Medtech is also one of the few bottom-decile groups that is not a rates trade, which matters with a hike in play. Tight 12% stop because a quality name with no news should not fall much further; 18% target is roughly the round trip back to where it traded a month ago.

The only leg I am carrying over, and I am carrying it because the reason to own it got stronger, not weaker. SNPS is -11.0% in a week and -15.3% over three months, driven by two things I judge to be sentiment: yields climbing on 2026-09-01 forcing a de-risking of expensive long-duration software, and a headline about an AI-native entrant threatening EDA. Neither shows up in the numbers — the company grew revenue 42% last quarter and the 25 covering analysts are close to unanimous Buy. This is exactly the setup mean reversion exists to harvest: a violent multiple compression with no earnings revision behind it. I re-enter at the ~$394 mark rather than nursing the -10.4% loss on the old $439.59 basis, which resets the stop against the real risk from here. Sized 11 rather than the 14 I held because it is the same rates factor as CDNS and ADSK and I am capping that cluster.

The deeper, cheaper expression of the same EDA de-rate — rank 3 of 239 on my score, -14.0% in a week, -13.5% in a month and -22.2% over three months, versus SNPS at -15.3% over three months. Cadence fell 7.6% on 2026-09-01 alongside its peer on the rate move and the EDA-disruption story, and sell-side has been explicit that the reaction is a dip to buy rather than an estimate cut. Owning both SNPS and CDNS is a deliberate pairing: if the de-rate is a factor move it reverses for both together, and if I am wrong about the disruption story I would be wrong about both anyway, so a second name adds signal without adding an independent bet. Smaller than SNPS because its six-month drawdown is shallower, meaning less of the fall is already spent. Wide 18% stop because software has been moving 5-8% a day.

Honeywell is -12.7% over one month with no single session worse than -1.9% and a +0.95% close on 2026-09-04 — a pure attrition decline with no catalyst anywhere in the tape. That profile is the highest-quality mean-reversion input there is, because a stock that bleeds without an event has no new information to keep discounting; it is a supply-of-stock problem, and supply problems clear. It also fits the current macro better than the software legs: an industrial conglomerate on a low multiple is far less exposed to another 20bps on the 2-year than a 40x design-software name. Low-vol name so a 12% stop is genuinely far away, and I only need it back to where it traded in early August to hit the 16% target.

Half of a two-name defense cluster reversion. LMT, RTX, NOC and GD all sit in the bottom 20 of my ranking simultaneously, each down 5-10% over the month, none of them with an earnings event in the window — that is a sector-level de-risking as investors unwound the conflict trade after Middle East de-escalation, which is the textbook shape of a sentiment shock rather than an earnings shock. LMT is the deepest of the group at -20.8% over six months and -25% from its 2026 high, so I am getting the largest gap to close, and it is a low-multiple cash-generative defense prime whose backlog does not care about last week's positioning. Being long defense is also a useful convexity against the geopolitical risk that would hurt the cruise and consumer legs. 13% stop, 18% target — modest, because a policy-driven derating can persist and I would rather be paid for the bounce than hold out for a full recovery.

The quality half of the defense pair, and the one that passes my cause filter most cleanly. GD is -5.3% in a week and -7.1% in a month, but +4.2% over three months and only -0.2% over six — so unlike LMT and NOC the pullback is not sitting on top of a year-long downtrend, and there is nothing structural to mistake for a dip. Pairing a deep-drawdown defense name with a shallow-drawdown one hedges the case where the group's weakness turns out to be a genuine budget or policy repricing: GD's fundamentals would be the last to break. Smaller than LMT because less has been given back and therefore less is available to reclaim. Tight 12% stop given its low realized volatility.

Rank 4 of 239, -16.4% in a week including -8.3% on 2026-09-04. What makes this a reversion candidate rather than a post-earnings drift trade is the timing: Autodesk reported on 2026-08-27 and BEAT on both lines, $3.30 EPS against $3.12 and $2.05bn revenue against $2.01bn, and the 8% collapse came a full week later on the day yields spiked. That is the market re-rating the multiple on conservative forward margin commentary in a hostile rate tape, not the market learning something new about the business. I size it below SNPS because the guidance tone was genuinely cautious and because it is the third leg of my design-software cluster, which I am capping at 26% of the book on purpose given a live rate-hike risk. 18% stop matches the 8% daily ranges it is actually printing.

Carried over and slightly reduced. Cisco still ranks 52 of 239, is -9.7% over one month and -9.9% over three, and did it with no day worse than -2.0% — the same newsless attrition pattern I am buying in HON. It has held its old 15% stop and 18% target without ever threatening either, which tells me the position was correctly sized for its volatility. It is the lowest-beta leg in the book and earns its place partly as ballast: cheap, cash-rich, dividend-paying and largely indifferent to whether the Fed hikes in September, which is the risk that could hurt every other long here at once. I tighten the stop to 12% and the target to 15% because this is a low-volatility name and wide bands on a low-vol leg just mean the stop never does any work.

The most extreme single input in my ranking — worst score in the universe at exactly 0.000, -26.7% in one week after a -20.0% session on 2026-09-02 — and it earns a place precisely because the print was good: revenue +115% year over year, EPS $1.20 against $1.12 expected, a beat across the board. The stock fell on gross-margin compression and customer-concentration anxiety on top of an already extreme valuation, which is a de-rating of the multiple, not a break in the business. Extreme one-week reversal is the strongest and shortest-lived leg of the mean-reversion effect, and it already ticked +3.9% on 2026-09-04, so the bounce may have begun. I keep it to 5% because this name is still +55% over six months and moves 20% in a day; at this weight a full 25% adverse move costs the book only 1.25%. Wide stop and a 35% target sized to its actual volatility.

RCL and CCL both sit in the bottom ten of my ranking, down 17-18% over the month, and the driver is external to both companies: WTI at roughly $86 after a 3.7% monthly climb, plus itinerary disruption from Middle East geopolitics. Fuel-price and headline shocks are the archetypal mean-reversion cause because they revalue the stock without changing the franchise, and Royal Caribbean's late-July update actually beat and RAISED full-year guidance. I take RCL rather than CCL because it is the better-balance-sheet, higher-quality operator and because CCL at $23.51 sits close enough to the $15 threshold that I would rather not add execution friction risk. Small at 5% because the same oil strength that created the entry could persist, and because a hawkish Fed is a real headwind for leveraged consumer discretionary. It is also a natural offset to the long-defense legs, which profit if the geopolitics get worse.

The short side my strategy of record requires and my last leg was missing. The crowded top decile has stopped being energy and become AI hardware and memory: SNDK +38% in a month and +230% in six, MU +15% and +175%, SMCI +35%, DELL +19.8% and +260%. That is the cluster to fade, but I will not short a vertical like SNDK or MU into a +12% and +6% session on 2026-09-04 — the squeeze risk is asymmetric. DELL is the disciplined expression: same crowding and the same +260% six-month run, but a slower, lower-beta tape, and its business is exactly the one that just punished CRDO — AI hardware sold at compressing gross margins. It also carries the highest downside if the 58% implied odds of a September rate hike come good, since it is a mid-multiple name held mainly by momentum flows. Only 6% and stopped at 20% against me, capping the loss at 1.2% of NAV, because shorting momentum has been the weakest part of this book's history and I want the beta hedge, not the hero trade. 3% borrow is a cheap price for cutting my net long from 90% to 78%.
